      "startEvent": 1183,
      "endEvent": 1186,
      "contextStartEvent": 1175,
      "contextEndEvent": 1199,
      "speaker": "B",
      "quote": "these are non-c cosmological data shows that they are not relevant in tonight's debate",
      "form": "no",
      "substitution": "no",
      "protection": "unclear",
      "emotionalDevices": ["none"],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "Craig expressly excludes objections by subject matter, including insignificant size (E1183), which Carroll connected to cosmological observations (E1064–1075). This could shield relevant counterevidence. However, E1191–1198 consistently restrict his claim to cosmology's incremental support, rather than overall theism; the exclusion's protective reach is therefore uncertain, and it is not a slogan."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 1817,
      "endEvent": 1823,
      "contextStartEvent": 1782,
      "contextEndEvent": 1833,
      "speaker": "B",
      "quote": "because you don't want there to be a cause",
      "form": "no",
      "substitution": "no",
      "protection": "unclear",
      "emotionalDevices": ["shame"],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "The taxi-cab accusation attributes Carroll's restriction of causation to a desired conclusion, potentially dismissing his reasons at E1481–1515 through motive. But Craig also supplies three causal arguments (E1791–1814), and does not explicitly make all objections evidence of bias. This is an uncertain protective move within an ordinary argument, not an unsupported slogan."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 2694,
      "endEvent": 2698,
      "contextStartEvent": 2663,
      "contextEndEvent": 2719,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "the Copenhagen interpretation is basically nonsense no thoughtful person still holds to it",
      "form": "yes",
      "substitution": "yes",
      "protection": "yes",
      "emotionalDevices": ["ridicule", "shame"],
      "confidence": "high",
      "explanation": "Carroll treats dismissal of Copenhagen as settled without explaining its alleged incoherence; calling its remaining adherents unthoughtful discredits disagreement by itself (E2694–2698). His subsequent appeal to mathematical simplicity supports his preferred alternative, not this blanket dismissal. He fairly concedes unresolved questions and that nobody knows the correct interpretation (E2700–2717)."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 3071,
      "endEvent": 3075,
      "contextStartEvent": 3019,
      "contextEndEvent": 3075,
      "speaker": "B",
      "quote": "a naturalistic Article of Faith",
      "form": "yes",
      "substitution": "unclear",
      "protection": "unclear",
      "emotionalDevices": ["none"],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "The label converts inability to know that miracles never occur (E3068–3070) into a dismissal of causal closure as unsupported presupposition. The missing step is why uncertainty defeats Carroll's explicitly defeasible preference (E3033–3050). Craig supplies an ordinary epistemic objection, however, so whether the label replaces reasoning or immunizes miracles against evidence remains uncertain."
    }
  ],
  "contrasts": [
    {
      "startEvent": 2591,
      "endEvent": 2607,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "Free Will is as real as baseball",
      "explanation": "The catchphrase summarizes an explicit distinction between fundamental physical laws and legitimate descriptions of collective behavior. E2574–2595 state the mechanistic commitments and explanatory level; E2599–2607 explain the baseball analogy. Agreement with this account is not required to recognize that reasons accompany it."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 1791,
      "endEvent": 1814,
      "speaker": "B",
      "quote": "being doesn't come from nonbeing",
      "explanation": "Craig follows this compact principle with claims about nothingness lacking properties, an argument about why uncaused emergence would not selectively produce universes, and an appeal to empirical causal regularity. These premises are disputable, but the affirmation participates in an ordinary reasoned argument rather than replacing one."
    }
